transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. What brings you to see me today?
I came in because I blew up at one of the younger volunteers over a crooked tablecloth. I don't usually talk to people that way, and it bothered me afterward.
Aside from feeling bothered by that incident, how has your overall mood been lately?
I’m not sure I’ve noticed much else, really. Mostly I just keep thinking about how I acted with that young man, and that doesn’t sit right with me.
Have you had other times where you lost your temper or had sudden outbursts like that?
No, not really. It was that incident with the volunteer—the crooked tablecloth—and I just blew up at him. That isn’t how I usually speak to people.
Do you generally feel a strong need for things to be arranged or done in a particular, orderly way?
I don’t think so. I mean, I like things to be decent, but I wouldn’t say I need everything arranged a certain way.
Have you noticed any problems with your memory recently?
I remember seeing the gun and the envelope on the sidewalk, but getting knocked down... that part is just gone. It’s like somebody cut it out of my memory.
Did you hit your head or lose consciousness during that event?
I—I don’t know. I remember the gun and that envelope on the sidewalk, but then the part where I got knocked down is just missing. Like somebody cut that piece right out.
Do you ever experience upsetting, unwanted memories or nightmares about that event with the gun?
Yes. Out of nowhere, I’ll hear that man’s rough voice in my head, or I’ll see that donation envelope hitting the ground again. It can happen when I’m just sitting at my kitchen table.
Do you find yourself going out of your way to avoid places, people, or activities that remind you of what happened?
Yeah. I’ve been taking the long way around so I don’t have to pass the bank. And I haven’t gone into the festival storage room either—it just brings the whole thing too close.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient experienced an armed robbery and physical assault, meeting criteria for a traumatic stressor. Following this event, the patient exhibits hallmark symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), including intrusive memories (vivid sensory recollections of the assailant's voice and envelope), active avoidance of trauma-related reminders (avoiding the bank and storage room), partial psychogenic/dissociative amnesia regarding the assault, and heightened irritability/anger outbursts.

confirmed_symptoms: Recurrent, involuntary, and distressing intrusive memories of the trauma (hearing the perpetrator's voice, seeing the envelope hit the ground)
Avoidance of external reminders of the event (taking the long route to avoid the bank, avoiding the festival storage room)
Inability to remember an important aspect of the traumatic event (memory gap around being knocked down)
Irritable behavior and angry outbursts with little or no provocation (blowing up at a volunteer over a tablecloth)

additional_requirements: Exposure to actual or threatened serious injury or violence (being confronted with a gun and knocked down)
